Seminar Title:

Fracture Performance Study of Concrete Incorporating Steel Slag and Polypropylene Fiber using Digital Image Correlation and Acoustic Emission

Seminar Type:

Speaker Name:

Sonali Bhowmik

Abstract:

Concrete is quasi-brittle and prone to cracking under monotonic and fatigue loading, making fracture performance crucial to structural integrity and service life. Steel slag (SS), an industrial by-product, can sustainably replace natural coarse aggregate, while chemically inert, inexpensive polypropylene (PP) fibers bridge microcracks and improve post-peak behavior. Their combined effect on fracture, particularly fracture process zone (FPZ) evolution under static and fatigue loading, remains unexplored. This thesis investigates this using digital image correlation (DIC) and acoustic emission (AE). Angular, rough-textured steel slag increased compressive strength and densified the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), while PP fibers improved tensile strength and elastic modulus and shifted failure from brittle to quasi-brittle. Under monotonic loading, 50% replacement improved fracture energy and peak load, whereas full replacement reduced characteristic length, increasing brittleness. PP fibers were beneficial up to 0.6%, beyond which agglomeration sharply reduced peak load and fracture energy. Fatigue tests on six mixes followed these trends all mixes showed the size effect, with partial replacement and fibres enlarging the FPZ and full replacement reducing it. DIC surface deformations quantified FPZ size, while AE energy, amplitude distribution, cumulative hits and an energy-based damage variable divided fracture into three stages: microcrack initiation, stable FPZ-governed crack propagation, and failure by macrocrack coalescence. PP fiber concrete produced more low-energy events, indicating delayed cracking. RA-AF analysis showed predominantly tensile (Mode-I) cracking, most pronounced in the optimum mix (50SS0.6). SHAP analysis ranked amplitude, then energy, average frequency, and counts as the most influential AE parameters for predicting fatigue fracture. XRD confirmed the weathered slag&rsquos mineralogical stability, ruling out volumetric expansion. SEM revealed the slag&rsquos rough, porous morphology and fiber pull-out, bridging, and crack deflection, while EDS showed Ca-Si-Fe enrichment and additional C-S-H gel at the ITZ, consistent with steel slag&rsquos latent hydraulic nature. Concrete with 50% steel slag and 0.6% PP fiber performed best in stiffness degradation, fracture toughness, crack growth rate, and FPZ size, with slag enhancing peak load and fibers improving post-peak softening and fatigue life. This combination offers a structurally efficient, sustainable option for fracture and fatigue-resistant concrete design.
